title: Iran watch
dek: Iranian oil exports under sanctions and naval blockade: tanker-tracked export estimates, floating storage, grades and rerouting, the shadow fleet, and China's buying. Every figure carries its vintage.

claims.text: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi detailed a seven-day Hormuz reopening plan in private meetings on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on September 25: hostilities would end on all fronts including Lebanon within seven days, the US would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen funds and waive oil sanctions, after which nuclear talks would resume. The White House said September 25 it was having positive and constructive conversations with mediators.
claims.source: The Hindu BusinessLine (citing the Associated Press)

claims.text: A senior Iranian official told Reuters on September 25 that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts the Hormuz proposal, and that the waterway would stay closed until all of Iran's conditions are met. Tehran would give no concessions on enriching uranium or shipping highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands. President Pezeshkian said he hopes for a deal before the November 3 midterm elections.
The current war was triggered February 28, 2026 by joint US and Israeli strikes on Iran; Iran responded by closing commercial access to Hormuz. The US blockaded Iranian ports from April 13.

The US blockade of Iranian ports started April 13, 2026; United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI) measures exports by vessels crossing the blockade line from the eastern point of Oman to the Iran-Pakistan border, exiting the Gulf of Oman, rather than by point of loading.

Mid-June 2026, the Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MOU) took effect and the US lifted the naval blockade under a sanctions waiver; Iran exported roughly 50 million barrels in the following two weeks (~1.66 million b/d in June, per TankerTrackers), and Iran's parliament speaker put the post-blockade figure above 40 million barrels.
In the 26 days after the MOU signing, Iran exported more than 80 million barrels of crude and products, worth over $6 billion at prevailing prices, per TankerTrackers.

Between the June 14 MOU announcement and July 6, Iran exported roughly 55 million barrels valued above $4.5 billion; pre-war, a typical month was 47-50 million barrels (~$3.05B), so the waiver window generated ~47% more revenue in 22 days than a full pre-war month.
Washington restored the blockade on July 14, 2026; Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers identified no Iranian crude cargo vessel successfully transiting Hormuz to China after that date.
claims.source: National Security Journal (citing Vortexa, Kpler, Reuters)

claims.text: On September 22, 2026, TankerTrackers spotted the first Iranian crude exports in two months: very large crude carriers (VLCCs) Diona (IMO 9569695) and Hero2 (IMO 9362073) plus the Suezmax tanker Sonia I exiting past the blockade line at the east end of the Gulf of Oman; Kpler confirmed four Iran-linked tankers exiting the Gulf of Oman.

Vessel-tracking data showed Iranian crude and condensate loadings averaged just 220,000 to 260,000 b/d in August 2026, down from 1.7 to 2.0 million b/d a year earlier, an over-80 percent collapse. No confirmed Iranian crude cargoes have passed the enforcement line since the US blockade went back up in mid-July, and analysts estimate production could fall to 1.2 to 1.3 million b/d if the blockade holds, near domestic consumption levels.
Iran's seaborne oil exports were 587 million barrels in 2024 (+10.75% y/y); China took 533 million barrels, 91% of the total, up 24% from 2023.
Iran exported 666 million barrels in 2025 (+13.5% y/y), with China by far the largest buyer.
March 2026 loadings were ~2.0 million b/d; July fell to ~749 kb/d of crude and condensate; August loadings were only ~220-255 kb/d.
claims.source: National Security Journal (citing Vortexa, Kpler, Reuters)

claims.text: May 2026 exports by sea were just 2.01 million barrels vs 29.7 million in April (-93%); the May total was four Panamax/Handymax naphtha shipments to China plus limited liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). Very large crude carrier (VLCC) 2-million-barrel crude shipments dropped to zero.

Iran's pre-war baseline exports were 1.68 million b/d; TankerTrackers estimated they had fallen to zero by early September 2026 and could remain there 'for the foreseeable future' depending on any agreement.

Iranian state media claimed August 2026 oil exports above $3 billion, the highest monthly figure in two years, sharply at odds with tracker estimates of ~220-255 kb/d loaded that month; treat as claimed, not tracked.
Iranian floating crude was ~29 million barrels on September 8, 2026, down from ~90 million in mid-July, the blockade drew down pre-war floating stock by roughly two-thirds (Kpler, via WSJ).
claims.source: WSJ via Kpler (compiled in Oil Depletion Report)

claims.text: Vortexa's broader measure, all Iranian crude stored aboard tankers, fell from ~135 million barrels at end-July to ~107 million by August 26; Iran is drawing down crude that had already cleared the blockade without replacing it.
Iran sold about 9 million barrels (~$900M) out of floating storage in the Gulf of Oman, vessels already clear of Iranian ports when enforcement began, hence outside the blockade's reach.

TankerTrackers estimated ~30 million barrels of Iranian crude awaiting export in mid-July, with ~60 million barrels of floating storage capacity available in surrounding waters as a buffer if production faced restrictions.

Iran's export stream is medium and heavy sour crude: Iran Light (medium sour, American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity 33.6, 1.46% sulfur) and Iran Heavy (heavy sour, API gravity about 29.5, sulfur about 1.77%), per National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) assays reported by S&P Global Platts.
claims.source: Hellenic Shipping News (citing S&P Global Platts)

claims.text: China's independent refiners buy mainly Iran Light and some Iran Heavy. They crack Iran Light directly in their crude distillation units; Iran Heavy has to be blended with lighter grades first.

Iran Light is a direct substitute for Russian Urals in China's teapot refineries (independent refiners): similar medium sour specs (Iran Light 33.6 API and 1.46% sulfur vs Urals 31.7 API and 1.19%), and teapot sources say Iranian barrels suit their units better than Russian ones.

Scarcity is already pricing in: Kpler reported Iran Light flipping from a $3.50 per barrel discount to a $3.50 premium over Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) Brent within a week as available floating cargoes thinned.

Kpler put total Iranian crude outside the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman at about 83 million barrels, with about 40 million at Singapore's Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) anchorage, but only about 4 million barrels of that still unsold. An unwind would mostly deliver already-sold cargoes, not flood the spot market.

The reroute path back is Kharg Island loadings, transit through the Gulf of Oman, ship-to-ship transfer at EOPL Malaysia, delivery to Shandong teapots. Kpler notes teapots have been substituting Russian Urals and fuel oil while Iranian barrels were blocked, with the Eastern Siberia-Pacific Ocean (ESPO) blend sold out weeks in advance.

So the grades hit hardest by a return are medium and heavy sours: Russian Urals first (direct teapot substitute), then the wider medium-sour complex. Light sweets are less exposed, though record ESPO premiums of $20 to $30 per barrel over Brent would also ease.

Bloomberg reported that the seized tankers Tiffany and Majestic X, both carrying Iranian crude, were tracked sailing along the Brazilian coast over the past week and are most likely headed for the United States, after several course changes since their seizure by US forces in April. The tanker Lenore, seized in the Indian Ocean in June, was spotted rounding the Cape of Good Hope west across the Atlantic; the combined cargo value of the three could reach $600 million.
UANI's 'ghost armada' reached 560 tracked tankers at end-2025 after 83 new vessels were identified during the year; of 180 tankers sanctioned in 2025, 108 had been previously identified by UANI.

TankerTrackers identified two US-sanctioned tankers in ballast that penetrated the blockade inbound for Iran with Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders on; the US Navy claims 13 Iranian tankers have been turned back so far.

During the June waiver window, 30+ tankers carrying 50M+ barrels of Iranian crude headed for Asia (Kpler); UANI separately tracked ~15 large Iranian-registered tankers departing Iranian ports with Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders switched on, a break from dark-fleet practice. For years, cargoes were masked via ship-to-ship (STS) transfers at Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits (EOPL) before continuing to Asia.

Treasury Secretary Bessent said the US sent warning letters to banks in China, Hong Kong, the UAE and Oman over continued Iranian-oil business, threatening secondary sanctions, 'the financial equivalent of a bomb' on Iran's oil sales system.

China imported ~431 million barrels of Iranian oil in 2023 (over 80% of Iran's exports), rising to ~533 million in 2024 (over 91%), largely via ghost-fleet tankers offloading through intermediaries before reaching China.
claims.source: Claire Jungman, UANI (House Foreign Affairs testimony)

claims.text: Treasury Secretary Bessent said June 29, 2026 that despite the US lifting sanctions on Iranian oil, no country except China had bought at a discount, others held back fearing sanctions snapback.

China is expected to remain the biggest buyer via independent refiners; UANI's Charlie Brown noted it was unclear whether exporters would abandon the established EOPL ship-to-ship transfer networks even under the waiver.
